title_en: Opening a Bank Account in America Can Really Pay You Over $10,000
excerpt_en: A newcomer in his forties opened his first US account at Chase and was offered $900 just for signing up. With more than 4,200 insured banks competing for customers, account bonuses are an industry, and they stack past $10,000.
body_en:
A newcomer to the United States, in his forties, walked into Chase — JPMorgan Chase — to open his first American bank account. Before the paperwork was even done, the bank put its offer on the table: $900 in bonuses, roughly 6,000 yuan. He applied entirely online, and a few days later a premium-looking debit card arrived in his mailbox.

In China, opening an account means asking the bank for a favor. In America, banks line up to pay you.

How the $900 Breaks Down

Chase's new-customer package is three bonuses stacked together:

  • Set up the checking account to receive your paycheck — one direct deposit from an employer earns $300;
  • Deposit $15,000 into the savings account and keep it there for 90 days — $200;
  • Do both, and Chase adds another $400 on top.

300 + 200 + 400 = 900. The conditions are printed in plain language, there are no hidden clauses, and when you meet them, the money lands.

Chase Is Not Being Unusually Generous

Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi — every major US bank runs account-opening bonuses, from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand. There are more than 4,200 federally insured deposit institutions in the United States, and dedicated websites track every live bonus offer in one table, so you can work through them bank by bank.

And deposit accounts are just the entry level. Credit-card sign-up bonuses and brokerage account offers pay even more. Line up all three — banks, cards, brokerages — and "over $10,000" stops being a headline and becomes simple addition. As the newcomer in the video puts it, with a bit of diligence and planning, the bonuses can basically cover a year of basic living costs.

Close the Account, Come Back, Get Paid Again

The best part: the wool grows back. Most US banks define a "new customer" right in their terms. At Chase, for example, if you have not received a similar account bonus in the past two years and have not had an account shut down by the bank, you count as new again. In other words, close the account, wait out the cooling-off period, and you can collect the same bonus a second time. The banks know exactly how this works — customer acquisition cost is simply a line item, and they have made their peace with it.

Why American Banks Pay You to Show Up

It comes down to competition. More than 4,200 institutions are fighting over the same customers; whoever does not pay does not get new accounts. And once a customer parks their paycheck, savings and credit cards with you, the decades of transaction flow, interest spread and fees that follow are the real prize — $900 to buy a customer's next thirty years is a trade any bank will make.

Compare that with China: a handful of giant banks, queues to open an account, transaction limits and frozen cards, and periodic campaigns against people who hold "too many" bank cards. The same act — opening an account — is banks begging you in a competitive market, and you begging the bank in a monopolized one.

(Compiled from a Douyin video by creator Yueheifeng Zaozhou documenting his account opening in the US. Bonus amounts and terms change; check each bank's current official terms.)
